objectives: Explain what the Ahî Organization was and when it appeared.
Describe the two possible roots of the word ‘Ahî’.
Explain why the Fütüvvet tradition comes next.
Use may, either … or, which and first … later.
content.pedagogy: A short opening chapter that defines the institution and its name. The two possible roots of the word show learners that historians sometimes give more than one possibility.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The book does not say which root is correct; it gives two possibilities.
The Ahî Organization was religious and social, not only a trade group.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: may (possibility) · either … or · which (relative) · first … later
Notice (Activity 1): may come from.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *may comes · *either … nor · *who means.
Use (Activity 4): where does a word come from?
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: a-HÎ, fü-tüv-VET.
Stress: in-sti-TU-tion, sig-NIF-i-cant, com-MER-cial, BROTH-er-hood.
beforeReading: Ask: “Do you know where your name comes from?”
duringReading: First reading: What was the Ahî Organization?
Second reading: complete a chart of the two roots.
Find what we must look at first.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Roots chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: word roots; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What kinds of life did the institution guide?
Why does the writer give two possible roots?
Why must we look at the Fütüvvet tradition first?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Anatolia, 13th Century” and “The Word ‘Ahî’” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: institution, appeared, significant, commercial, highlights.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the two words written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short dictionary entry for the word ‘Ahî’.

expectedResponses: The Ahî Organization was a religious and social institution that appeared in Anatolia in the 13th century. The word ‘Ahî’ may come either from the Old Turkish ‘akı’ (generous and brave) or from the Arabic ‘ah’ (brother).
content.transferTask: Write about a word or name and its possible roots.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners understand that the writer gives two possibilities?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “may” and one with “either … or”.

objectives: Describe how the Fütüvvet tradition changed over time.
Explain the meaning of ‘fetâ’.
Explain how Fütüvvet reached Anatolia and became the Ahî movement.
Use time phrases (by, later, in its final stage) and turn into.
content.pedagogy: A history of an idea in stages. A time line helps learners follow the many changes: a quality → a youth movement → a Sufi identity → an official organization → a professional group.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Fütüvvet started in the first century of Islam; the word ‘fetâ’ comes from the pre-Islamic period.
The Ahî movement is the Anatolian form of Fütüvvet, not a different idea.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: time phrases (by + time, later, in its final stage) · turn into · take on · but / however
Notice (Activity 1): turned into.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the time phrases, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *Since the 9th century (meaning) · *turned to an organized movement.
Use (Activity 4): how something changed.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: fü-tüv-VET, fe-TÂ, ab-BA-sid.
Stress: gen-er-OS-i-ty, BRAV-er-y, pro-FES-sion-al, AR-ti-san.
beforeReading: Ask: “Can an idea change over hundreds of years? Give an example.”
duringReading: First reading: Where did Fütüvvet start?
Second reading: make a time line of five stages.
Find how it reached Anatolia.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Time line; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: how something changed; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What qualities did ‘fetâ’ describe?
How did the Sufi movement change Fütüvvet?
What stayed the same in the final stage?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Fetâ” and “The Abbasids” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: qualities, artisan class, spirit.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the time line with the dates written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph about the stages with four time phrases.

expectedResponses: Fütüvvet started in the first century of Islam. By the 9th century, it turned into a youth movement and took on a Sufi identity. Later, it became an official organization and finally joined the artisans. It reached Anatolia through the Abbasids.
content.transferTask: Write about how a tradition or a place changed over time.
content.teacherReflection: Did the time line help learners follow the stages?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “By the … century” and one with “turned into”.

objectives: Explain why the Caliph sent a Fütüvvet robe to the Sultan.
Describe the role of Sühreverdî.
Explain what changed for the Fütüvvet groups.
Use by + -ing, because of this, as a result and passive participles.
content.pedagogy: A political chapter: a gift (the robe) has a meaning (official recognition and control). A cause-result chain helps learners follow the Caliph’s plan.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The robe did not make the Sultan the leader of the Caliph; it showed that the Caliph accepted the Sultan’s power.
Sühreverdî was the Caliph’s messenger and advisor, not the Sultan.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: by + -ing (method) · because of this · as a result · past participles (sent by the Caliph) · past passive
Notice (Activity 1): By establishing it …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *By establish · *sending by the Caliph.
Use (Activity 4): a gift with a meaning.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: â-lâ-ed-DİN key-ku-BAD, nâ-SIR li-dî-nil-LÂH, şe-hâ-bed-DİN es-süh-re-ver-DÎ.
Stress: CAL-iph /ˈkeɪlɪf/, CER-e-mo-ny, stra-TE-gic.
beforeReading: Ask: “Can a gift be a political message? How?”
duringReading: First reading: What did the Caliph send, and to whom?
Second reading: make a chain: plan → messenger → ceremony → result.
Find what the robe showed.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Cause-result chain; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a gift with a meaning; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the Caliph choose Sühreverdî?
What did the Caliph want from the Fütüvvet groups?
What did the ceremony in Konya show?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Fütüvvet Robe” and “Konya” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: robe, previously, welcomed.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chain with the first and last boxes filled.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the scene in Konya as a short news report.

formativeAssessment: Uses by + -ing or as a result correctly.
expectedResponses: The Caliph wanted to make Fütüvvet an official institution to get its political support. He sent Sühreverdî to Konya, where he dressed Keykubad in the robe sent by the Caliph. As a result, the Caliph officially accepted Keykubad’s power.
content.transferTask: Write about a gift or object that has a special meaning.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see the robe as a political message?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “By + -ing” and one with “As a result”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses by + -ing or as a result.

content.chapter: Chapter 4: Ahî Evran and the Spread of the Ahîs
objectives: Describe Ahî Evran and his role in Anatolia.
Explain how the Ahîs became powerful when the government was weak.
Describe the Ahîs’ role against Gıyâseddin II and the Mongols.
Use who clauses, known as, the past perfect and although.
content.pedagogy: A chapter of people, places and political events. A map of Ahî Evran’s route (Denizli, Konya, Kayseri, Kırşehir) and a short time line (Keykubad I → Gıyâseddin II → Kösedağ → Kayseri) make it clear.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Ahî Evran came from Central Asia; he settled in Kırşehir, not in Konya.
The Ahîs defended Kayseri, but the city finally fell.
The text says “It is believed”; the poisoning is not stated as a proven fact.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: who (non-defining) · known as … · past perfect (had supported) · it is believed that · although
Notice (Activity 1): although the city finally fell.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *which played a key role (person) · *Knowing as · *has supported (past).
Use (Activity 4): helping in difficult times.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: a-HÎ ev-RAN, kır-şe-HİR, kö-se-DAĞ, gı-yâ-sed-DİN.
Stress: NO-mad-ic, in-VA-sion, SPIR-it-u-al.
beforeReading: Ask: “What happens in a town when there is no government or order?”
duringReading: First reading: Who was Ahî Evran?
Second reading: draw his route on a map.
Make a time line of the political events.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Map and time line; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: helping in difficult times; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why was Ahî Evran important for artisans?
Why did the Ahîs become powerful in weak times?
Why did the Ahîs oppose Gıyâseddin II?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Kırşehir” and “Kösedağ” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: nomadic, suspected, supported, poisoned, defeated, defend, fell.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the map with the four cities marked.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short biography of Ahî Evran with two who clauses.

formativeAssessment: Explains the Ahîs’ power in weak times.
Uses although or a who clause correctly.
expectedResponses: Ahî Evran, who came from Central Asia, settled in Kırşehir and founded a zaviye for artisans. When the government was weak, the Ahîs took control of city governments, and they helped defend Kayseri against the Mongols, although the city finally fell.
content.transferTask: Write about people who helped their town in a difficult time.
content.teacherReflection: Did the map and time line make the chapter clear?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “who” about Ahî Evran and one with “although”.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: Values and Way of Life
objectives: Describe the duties of the organization in business life.
Explain the rules of the Fütüvvet way of life.
Explain the role of the Fütüvvetnâmeler.
Use are expected to, should, must and such as.
content.pedagogy: The chapter moves from the economic duties of the organization to the personal rules of its members. A two-column chart (business / behavior) shows how work and character were connected.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Fütüvvetnâmeler are guidebooks, not laws of the state.
Tekkes and zaviyes are Sufi places, not shops.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: be expected to · should · must · such as · passive (were written down)
Notice (Activity 1): are expected to.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *should to have · *must helps · *such like.
Use (Activity 4): a guidebook for my class.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: fü-tüv-vet-nâ-me-LER, tek-KE, zâ-vi-YE.
Stress: GEN-er-ous, THANK-ful, PER-ma-nent, do-NA-tions.
beforeReading: Ask: “What rules should a good shop owner follow?”
duringReading: First reading: What did the organization do in business life?
Second reading: complete the chart: business / behavior.
Find where the values were written down.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a guidebook for my class; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How did the organization help business life?
Which rule of the Fütüvvet way of life do you find most important?
Why should followers remember that this world is not permanent?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Fütüvvetnâmeler” and “Masters and Apprentices” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: tekkes, zaviyes, goods, treat workers well, forbidden, permanent, making donations.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with one item in each column.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short Fütüvvetnâme for modern workers with five rules.

expectedResponses: The Ahî Organization solved trade problems, checked quality and set prices. Its rules were written in the Fütüvvetnâmeler: followers were expected to be generous, honest and thankful, to treat workers well and to avoid forbidden behaviors.
content.transferTask: Write rules for a class guidebook.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect work and character?

exitTicket: Write one rule with “are expected to” and one with “must”.

content.chapter: Chapter 6: Education in the Ahî Organization
objectives: Describe the qualities of Ahî role models.
Explain why seeking knowledge was a basic rule.
Describe the levels of Ahî training and the role of the zaviyes.
Use must, if-clauses, therefore and as a result.
content.pedagogy: Education is at the heart of the chapter: role models, seeking knowledge, levels of training and the zaviyes as schools. Learners can compare Ahî education with education today.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Apprentices did not become masters directly; there was a level in between.
Zaviyes were not only for religion; they acted as schools and cultural centers.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: must · if + present, must + verb · therefore · as a result · act as / serve as
Notice (Activity 1): If a person does not have the skills …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *must to learn · *If a person will not have.
Use (Activity 4): my role model.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: zâ-vi-YE, ha-LAL.
Stress: MOD-est, ED-u-cat-ed, ap-PREN-tices, WORLD-view.
beforeReading: Ask: “Who taught you how to behave? How did they teach you?”
duringReading: First reading: What makes a good role model?
Second reading: list the levels of training.
Find what zaviyes acted as.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Qualities and levels; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: my role model; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why were role models important?
Why did not learning a job properly bring shame?
How were zaviyes similar to schools today?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Role Models” and “Zaviyes as Schools” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: Role models, staying modest, avoiding, encourage, deeds, prevent, in essence, worldview, served as, grew.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a list of role-model qualities to tick while reading.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Compare Ahî education and education today in a short paragraph.

expectedResponses: Role models had to be modest, pray and earn a halal living. Seeking knowledge was a basic rule, so young people learned from masters and went through levels until they became masters. Zaviyes acted as schools for the people of Anatolia.
content.transferTask: Write about a role model in your life.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners compare Ahî education with their own?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “If …, … must …” and one with “Therefore”.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: The Ahîs and the Ottoman State
objectives: Explain the role of the Ahîs in the formation of the Ottoman Empire.
Describe how the organization lost its political power.
Report the views of historians and Ibn Battuta.
Use not only … but also, reporting verbs and however.
content.pedagogy: The chapter moves from the Ahîs’ political and military role to their later economic role, and closes with Ibn Battuta’s praise. Learners practice separating the writer’s claims from reported views.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Ahîs were one of four main forces, not the only force.
After Mehmed II, the organization did not disappear; it managed business affairs.
Ibn Battuta was a traveler from Tangier, not an Ottoman official.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: not only … but also · reporting verbs (say that, note that) · however · from that time on
Notice (Activity 1): not only in education but also …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *not only … but too · *Historical sources tell that.
Use (Activity 4): something unique in my region.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: MU-rad, meh-MED, ib-ni bat-TU-ta, TAN-gier /tænˈdʒɪr/.
Stress: for-MA-tion, vi-ZIERS, POL-i-tics, u-NIQUE.
beforeReading: Ask: “What do travelers often write about the places they visit?”
duringReading: First reading: What role did the Ahîs play in the Ottoman Empire?
Second reading: make a before / after chart for Mehmed II.
Find what Ibn Battuta said.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Before / after chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: something unique; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why were the Ahîs important for the early Ottomans?
What changed after Mehmed II?
Why did Ibn Battuta call the organization unique?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Murad I” and “Ibn Battuta” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: note, managed, business affairs, artisan, Indeed, unique, attributes.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with “before” filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short summary of the whole book using not only … but also.

formativeAssessment: Describes the change after Mehmed II.
Uses not only … but also correctly.
expectedResponses: The Ahîs were one of the four main forces that helped build the Ottoman Empire, and Murad I joined the organization. From the rule of Mehmed II, it lost its political power. Ibn Battuta said that the organization was unique in the world.
content.transferTask: Write about something unique in your region.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners separate the writer’s claims from reported views?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “not only … but also” and one with “Historians note that …”.

objectives: Describe the joining ceremonies of the Ahî order.
Explain the symbolic meaning of the belt.
Explain the seven pairs of doors in plain words.
Use imperatives, mean / represent and that is to say.
content.pedagogy: A symbolic chapter: drinking şerbet and wearing a belt carried moral meanings. The list of seven doors turns values into clear advice. The jigsaw closes the book by bringing all chapters together.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The belt is a symbol; the doors are not real doors.
The ceremonies were for joining the organization, not for weddings.
The list lines belong to the teacher-approved text and are read as they are.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: imperatives in pairs · mean / represent · each + singular verb · that is to say
Notice (Activity 1): Close the door … and open the door …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then explain the symbols.
Likely errors: *Each of these represent · *That is say.
Use (Activity 4): my doors to close and open.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Words: şer-BET, peş-ta-MAL, şal-VAR.
Stress: STIN-gi-ness, gen-er-OS-i-ty, PA-tience, re-PENT-ance.
beforeReading: Ask: “Do you know a ceremony where clothes or objects have a special meaning?”
duringReading: First reading: What happened in the joining ceremonies?
Second reading: make a chart: close / open.
Find what the belt represents.
afterReading: Group task: “The Ahî Way: Then and Now”.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–18 Close / open chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–34 Language Focus 1–3; 34–42 Use: my doors; 42–45 Exit ticket. (Jigsaw in a second lesson.)
discussionPoints: Why did the ceremonies use objects like a belt?
Which pair of doors is most important for you?
How do the seven doors connect with the values in Chapter 5?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Şerbet” and “The Belt” when the picture is in place.
The group task “The Ahî Way: Then and Now” closes the book.
Word Notes: distinct, manner of behavior.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the “close” column filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph explaining three pairs in plain words.

formativeAssessment: Explains the meaning of the belt.
expectedResponses: Joining the Ahî organization included drinking şerbet and wearing a traditional belt. The belt had seven names, seven rules and seven meanings: close the door of a bad habit, such as anger, and open the door of a good one, such as patience.
content.transferTask: Write four pairs of advice in the style of the Ahî belt.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners turn the symbols into clear values?

exitTicket: Write one pair: “Close the door of … and open the door of …”.

metadata.title: The Ahî Organization B1 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: The Ahî Organization (Ahilik)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 8 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow connected texts about history, society and values, and who can produce supported explanations and short reflections.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the history of the Ahî Organization: its Fütüvvet roots, its role among the Seljuks and Ottomans, its values, education and ceremonies, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 8 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a map, a date or a picture.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: definition, stages, cause and result, rules, or reported views.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practice it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: may (possibility) · either … or · which (relative) · first … later
Ch2: time phrases (by + time, later, in its final stage) · turn into · take on · but / however
Ch3: by + -ing (method) · because of this · as a result · past participles (sent by the Caliph) · past passive
Ch4: who (non-defining) · known as … · past perfect (had supported) · it is believed that · although
Ch5: be expected to · should · must · such as · passive (were written down)
Ch6: must · if + present, must + verb · therefore · as a result · act as / serve as
Ch7: not only … but also · reporting verbs (say that, note that) · however · from that time on
Ch8: imperatives in pairs · mean / represent · each + singular verb · that is to say

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, people, places and key events.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify main ideas, stages, causes and results, rules and reported views.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: describe people and institutions, explain rules and causes, and report views.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce connected B1 paragraphs using evidence, linking words and chapter patterns.

valuesFocus: D6 Honesty — Honest work and honest words.
D3 Diligence — Learning a job well through training.
D20 Helpfulness — Sharing with and supporting others.
D14 Respect — Respect for elders, scholars and masters.
languageFocus: Every one of the 8 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the thinking target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, picture cards, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for one more sentence or one more reason from the book, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.
Chapter 4 says “It is believed that he was poisoned by his son.” Present it as a belief, as the book does.
Bracketed Turkish words in the text belong to the teacher-approved story; they are read as they are.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The Ahî Organization links medieval Anatolia with questions every community faces today: how to do honest work, how to train young workers and how to help people in need.

themes.title: Honest work:
themes.description: The organization checked the quality of goods and set prices (Chapter 5). Discuss how customers are protected today.

themes.title: Learning from a master:
themes.description: Young people went from apprentice to master (Chapter 6). Compare this with vocational training today.

themes.title: Sharing and helping:
themes.description: Followers shared food, treated workers well and made donations (Chapter 5). Discuss how people support each other in your community.

themes.title: Admired by travelers:
themes.description: Ibn Battuta said that the organization was unique in the world (Chapter 7). Discuss what visitors admire in your region.

actions: Find one shop or workshop in your area and write two sentences about what it makes.
Make a short poster: “Five rules for a good worker”.
Ask an older family member how they learned their job.

exitTicket: One idea from today’s chapter, with the sentence that supports it, is …
One language pattern I noticed today, and what it does in the sentence, is …
One action I can take this week that shows a value from the chapter is …

miniProject.title: The Ahî Way: Then and Now
miniProject.desc: In groups, each member becomes an expert on one part of the book: history, values, education or ceremonies. Teach your part, then make a poster with three Ahî ideas that are useful today, each with a sentence from the book.

reflectivePrompt.title: Doors to Close and Open
reflectivePrompt.desc: The Ahî belt asks members to close the door of a bad habit and open the door of a good one (Chapter 8). Write six to eight sentences about one habit you would like to change. What will you close, what will you open, and how?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D6 Honesty
items.value: Honesty: Followers were expected to be honest, and the organization checked the quality of goods (Chapter 5).

items.label: D3 Diligence
items.value: Diligence: Young people went through levels from apprentice to master, and seeking knowledge was a basic rule (Chapter 6).

items.label: D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Helpfulness: Followers shared food, treated workers well and made donations (Chapter 5).

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Respect: Members spent time with wise elders and built close relations with scholars (Chapters 5 and 6).

questions: What small action can show it this week?
Which part is from the book and which part is my own idea?

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR B1. The table links the B1 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test B1 to the chapters of this book where learners practice them.

rows.descriptor: Can read straightforward factual texts on subjects related to his/her field and interest with a satisfactory level of comprehension.
practice: Chapter 2 (The Fütüvvet Tradition): Put the stages of Fütüvvet in order.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write straightforward connected texts on a range of familiar subjects within his field of interest, by linking a series of shorter discrete elements into a linear sequence.
practice: Chapter 5 (Values and Way of Life): Write rules for a class guidebook.
Chapter 7 (The Ahîs and the Ottoman State): Write about something unique in your region.
Language Review, “Use: An Organization That Helps People”: Write six to eight sentences.

rows.descriptor: Can reasonably fluently sustain a straightforward description of one of a variety of subjects within his/her field of interest, presenting it as a linear sequence of points.

test.title: End-of-Level Test B1
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B1 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 70 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (45 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (25 minutes): on paper. Write an article for your school website about a person you admire. (100–130 words)
Speaking (about 8 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

metadata.title: The Ahî Organization B1 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 25 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B1 learners who study the Ahî Organization alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 8 chapters of The Ahî Organization.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Follow the roots, history and role of the Ahî Organization.
Explain its values, education and ceremonies with evidence from the book.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 8.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One Ahî rule that I would like to follow:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 8 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 25 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows honesty, hard work, helpfulness and respect. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Honesty: Honesty: Followers were expected to be honest, and the organization checked the quality of goods (Chapter 5).
Diligence: Diligence: Young people went through levels from apprentice to master, and seeking knowledge was a basic rule (Chapter 6).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: Followers shared food, treated workers well and made donations (Chapter 5).
Respect: Respect: Members spent time with wise elders and built close relations with scholars (Chapters 5 and 6).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 8, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell someone at home in five sentences what the Ahî Organization was, in your home language or in English.
